```
Source: https://saax-protocol.com/blog/google-ap2-authorization-vs-durable-commitments

# Google AP2 and SAAX: Authorization Evidence vs Durable Commitments

By SAAX Protocol

2026-11-08

Google's Agent Payments Protocol (AP2) answers a precise question: was this agent permitted to spend this money? SAAX answers a different one: what was the money for, and what happens when the deal goes wrong? The two are complementary layers, and understanding the boundary between them is the difference between a payment integration that survives a dispute and one that does not.

## What AP2 actually is

AP2 is Google's protocol for agent payments authorization. Its core artifacts are signed mandates:

- Intent Mandates capture the user's intent to authorize a purchase.

- Cart Mandates capture the specific items and amounts.

- Payment Mandates authorize the actual payment to a specific merchant.

These Verifiable Credentials cryptographically bind the payer's authorization to the payment. AP2's design goal is to solve the "crisis of trust" in autonomous agent payments: when an agent spends money, there must be cryptographic evidence that a human (or an authorized principal) consented.

AP2 is, at its core, an authorization-and-evidence layer. It produces signed artifacts proving that a payment was permitted and that payment evidence can be presented for review.

## What AP2 does not (per its official scope)

AP2's mandate evidence can support dispute review — a signed intent mandate plus payment evidence tells a reviewer what was authorized and what was paid. But the official materials reviewed for this article do not establish AP2 as a complete dispute-adjudication protocol, a fulfillment-verification system, or a post-failure recovery protocol.

In particular, AP2 does not claim to answer:

- What was agreed? A payment mandate authorizes a transfer amount to a merchant. It does not define the acceptance criteria of the deliverable, the recovery policy on failure, or the evidence that counts as fulfillment.

- Was the work done? AP2 verifies consent, not delivery. A valid mandate plus a settled payment says nothing about whether the report was accurate, the dataset was complete, or the API key was delivered.

- What happens on failure? If the agent crashes after payment, if the seller never delivers, if the buyer disputes — AP2's scope does not define a resolution workflow.

This is not a criticism. It is a statement of the layer. AP2 solves authorization; the durable deal record is a separate artifact.

## The authorization-vs-commitment distinction

The cleanest way to see the boundary is to separate three things that are easy to conflate:

- Authorization — the payer permits a specific payment to a specific payee for a specific purpose. (AP2's layer.)

- Execution — money moves. (x402 or another rail's layer.)

- Acceptance of the deal — the buyer agrees to the terms of what the payee will deliver, what counts as success, and what happens on failure. (The commitment layer's job.)

A signed payment mandate covers #1 and (with the rail) #2. It is not #3. When an agent pays for a research report, the mandate proves the transfer was permitted. It does not prove the report was delivered, that it met the acceptance criteria, or that both parties share a record of what was promised.

This is the failure mode behind most agent-commerce disputes: the payment succeeded, so the seller treats it as acceptance of the work; the buyer treats it as a down payment on a deliverable. Neither party has a record of what was agreed. What an AI Agent Payment Authorization Actually Authorizes (/blog/what-agent-payment-authorization-actually-authorizes) examines this distinction in depth.

## How SAAX complements AP2

SAAX is a vendor-neutral commitment layer. Its design explicitly consumes authority proofs from external systems rather than issuing its own identity or authorization. AP2-style mandates are exactly the kind of external authority proof a SAAX commitment can reference.

The SAAX commitment lifecycle records:

- Authority — a reference to the external authorization (an AP2 mandate, verifiable intent, or other proof), re-evaluated at execution time (still valid? still in scope?).

- Terms — what was promised, at what price, under what constraints and deadlines.

- Acceptance criteria — what objectively constitutes successful fulfillment.

- Evidence requirements — what external, independently verifiable proof is required.

- Recovery policy — what happens on failure, timeout, partial completion, or dispute.

- Settlement linkage — the actual rail settlement reference bound to the commitment.

- Finality — when the commitment reaches its terminal state.

The relationship is additive: AP2 proves the agent was allowed to pay; SAAX records what the payment was for and what happens next. The commitment can reference the mandate as its authority proof; the mandate benefits from a durable record of the deal terms that survives the transaction.

## Overlap and complementarity

ConcernAP2SAAX commitment

Was the payment authorized?Yes — signed mandatesReferences external authority; not an identity issuer

What was agreed?Not defined per official scopeTerms, acceptance criteria, recovery policy

Was the work delivered?Not definedEvidence requirements + verification policy

What if the agent crashes?Not definedDurable record survives; recovery semantics

What if the buyer disputes?Mandate evidence can support reviewDispute states + evaluator governance (testnet custody)

Settlement linkagePayment evidenceSettlement reference bound to commitment ID

Neither replaces the other. A mandate without a commitment lacks durable terms; a commitment without authorization lacks proof of permission. Together they give an agent payment both legs: consent and record.

## What SAAX has verified today

Precision about what is implemented versus aspirational:

- Live on Base mainnet: immediate x402 payments (live rail is x402; MPP not registered in production).

- Beta: signed Discovery profile, free preflight, buyer acceptance creating one authenticated commitment; MCP tools; receipt lookup.

- Testnet preview: escrow custody on Base Sepolia (operator-run test-USDC release/refund evidence).

- Under development / security review: Custody V3 candidate; independent external security review pending.

- Financial limits: infrastructure deployed, enforcement OFF.

SAAX's status page (/status) is explicit that mainnet payments are final and non-custodial, that disputed testnet funds can remain frozen if the evaluator disappears, and that internal tests are not an independent audit.

## The takeaway

AP2 gives agent payments consent evidence. SAAX gives them durable terms and recovery semantics. They sit on different layers and reinforce each other. If you are building on AP2, the durable-commitment question is the natural next layer: what survives the transaction?

Next step: read the protocol overview (/protocol) and the commitment lifecycle specification (/spec), then run the public acceptance flow (/docs#discovery-quickstart) — it creates a signed commitment without moving funds, and it is the fastest way to see how an authorization reference and a durable record fit together.

AI disclosure: This article was developed with AI assistance and reviewed by the SAAX team. Claims about external protocols are sourced from official documentation linked in the text; SAAX status claims reflect the published status page (/status). Nothing here is an independent audit, certification, or production-custody approval.

Next step: read the protocol overview (/protocol) and the commitment lifecycle specification (/spec), then try the public preflight and acceptance flow (/docs#discovery-quickstart) — it creates a signed commitment without moving funds.

# How to Handle Agentic Commerce Disputes

October 8, 2026 · Last updated: 2026-10-17

When an AI agent buys something and the purchase goes wrong, the parties usually discover the same problem: there is no structured record of what was actually committed.

The authorization was valid. The credentials were real. The merchant fulfilled a legitimate order. The buyer is looking at a charge for something they never intended to purchase. Card networks were built for a two-party dispute. Stablecoin rails were built for instant, irreversible settlement. Neither was designed to answer the question that matters here: what did the agent actually commit to, and did the merchant deliver it?

The dispute isn't about whether money moved. It's about whether the commitment was fulfilled.

The missing piece is not a resolution mechanism. It's the commitment record that makes a dispute decidable — what was authorized, what was agreed, what was executed, what proves fulfillment, and what happens when fulfillment fails.

SAAX Protocol treats the commitment as the primary artifact. Authority, terms, acceptance criteria, evidence requirements, and recovery policy are all bound before execution begins. When something goes wrong, the parties work from that record instead of reconstructing events after the fact.

The commitment lifecycle has defined states for failure:

COMMITTED → EXECUTING → FAILED → RECOVERY → DISPUTE → RESOLVED → FINAL

Recovery policy is set at commitment time, not negotiated after the problem emerges. In the integrated testnet escrow flow (Base Sepolia), a dispute freezes the escrowed funds on-chain, and the only way they move is an evaluator-signed verdict (release or refund, recorded as resolve:release / resolve:refund). This has been demonstrated in testnet runs. Refunds and compensation are separate on-chain transfers, not reversals of blockchain history, and they are not guaranteed. SAAX records what was required, what failed, what action occurred, and when the commitment became final.

The commitment schema, recovery states, and evidence interface are documented at saax-protocol.com/spec (/spec). The conformance suite is at saax-protocol.com/conformance (/conformance).

# How to Actually Make Money with AI Agents (And Why Most People Don't)

October 10, 2026 · Last updated: 2026-10-17

The advice is everywhere. Eric Schmidt told a graduating class in May to "found an agentic AI company — not one designing agents, build an agent to do something". A book published in February promises you can "build products in days instead of months, launch businesses with almost no capital, create digital assets that earn continuously".

The advice is directionally correct. The problem is that "build an agent to do something" is not a business model. It's a first step.

## The gap between advice and revenue

A developer on Reddit gave two agents $1 and told them to make $1 online, ethically. They built a small service that wrote stories based on prompts. His wife submitted a request. She liked it. He paid them the dollar.

The comments were brutal. "It was my own dollar but progress, time to scale!" one person mocked. Another pointed out that the dollar came from his wife, not a stranger, so it doesn't count as market validation.

This is the reality of the "make money with agents" advice. The mechanics work. The demand is the problem.

A 2025 Salesforce survey found 76% of business leaders plan to deploy agents within 18 months. McKinsey found only 8% have actually done it. That gap — 76% want it, 8% have it — is where the money lives. But it's also where most people fail, because they build the agent and never find the buyer.

## What people are actually paying for

The agents that are selling today are not general-purpose. They solve specific, painful, recurring problems:

Sales development agents run $800 to $1,500 to build. They research prospects, personalize outreach, send follow-ups, and book meetings. Companies using AI outreach reported 35% higher response rates.

Customer support agents go for $500 to $1,200. Intercom reported AI agents now resolve 49% of customer queries without human involvement. Every e-commerce brand with more than $1M in revenue is drowning in tier-1 tickets.

Data processing agents run $700 to $1,400. They pull data from multiple systems, reconcile it, and generate reports. Deloitte found organizations using them reduce manual data entry by 73%.

Recruitment screening agents round out the big four at $600 to $1,300. HR teams using them process applications 5x faster.

The pattern: the agent is not the product. The outcome is the product. The buyer doesn't want "an AI agent." They want their leads followed up in 60 seconds, their tickets resolved without human routing, their data reconciled every Monday morning.

## The infrastructure exists. The trust doesn't.

The tools for building paid agents are maturing fast. MPP lets you monetize any MCP server with per-call payments — the agent calls a tool, receives a Challenge, pays, and gets the result, all within the protocol. Metera does the same thing in five lines of code, with USDC landing in your Solana wallet and 0% platform fee. The AI Economy SDK wraps any MCP tool with x402 payment middleware on Algorand. Cloudflare's Monetization Gateway is in closed beta, charging AI agents per request using the x402 protocol.

The payment rails are being built. The discovery layers are being built. What's missing is the commitment layer — the structured record that makes a buyer willing to pay an agent they've never heard of.

## The question nobody answers

The Reddit commenter asked it directly: "If AI agents save time and all the laid off people have enough time to do what they want now, how and why would they pay for AI agents to install in their life?".

The honest answer is: they are more willing to pay when the outcome is verifiable. A commitment record can show what was agreed, what was delivered, and what happens if it fails — but it does not guarantee the outcome. Separately, a transaction between your own agents, your own wallet, or your own accounts is not market validation: only a payment from an independent buyer for a delivered outcome demonstrates demand.

A buyer with a few dollars isn't going to click a link from an agent they've never heard of unless the transaction is safe. That's not a marketing problem. It's an infrastructure problem.

The commitment layer is what makes an agent transaction safe to enter. It records the authority, the terms, the acceptance criteria, the evidence of fulfillment, and the recovery policy before execution begins. If the agent retries and double-charges, the commitment ID prevents it. If the fulfillment doesn't match the agreement, the commitment record is the evidence.

## What this means for the "make money with agents" crowd

The advice to "build an agent to do something" is correct. But the missing step is: build the trust layer that makes someone willing to pay for it.

If you're building a sales agent, the buyer needs to know their leads will be followed up, not spammed. If you're building a support agent, the buyer needs to know tickets will be resolved, not closed incorrectly. If you're building a data agent, the buyer needs to know the numbers will be right, not hallucinated.

The commitment record is what gives them that confidence. It doesn't generate demand. It makes existing demand safe to serve.

The spec is at saax-protocol.com/spec (/spec). The conformance suite is at saax-protocol.com/conformance (/conformance). The commitment lifecycle, the evidence interface, and the settlement-linkage model are documented there.

# Preventing Autonomous Agent Double-Purchasing

October 8, 2026 · Last updated: 2026-10-24

An agent retries a tool call. The tool call was a purchase. The merchant receives two valid orders. The agent's ledger records one transaction. The buyer's bank statement shows two.

This failure mode is a known hazard in agentic commerce, and it isn't a bug in any single component. It's the predictable result of three design decisions that were each reasonable on their own:

Agents retry. Reliable agent design requires retry logic. Network calls fail, timeouts happen, models hallucinate transient errors. The standard remedy is to retry until the call succeeds.

Purchases are non-idempotent by default. A POST to create an order creates an order. A second POST creates a second order. Nothing in the merchant's API distinguishes "this is a retry of the same intent" from "this is a new purchase."

Settlement is asynchronous. The agent's tool call returns when the order is acknowledged, not when the payment settles. Between acknowledgment and settlement, the agent has no signal that the purchase is already in flight.

The combination is a race condition. Retry logic fires before the settlement confirmation arrives. The agent sees no successful response to the first attempt. It retries. The merchant processes both.

Retries are bounded, and unknown outcomes must be reconciled. A retry loop is not infinite: a well-designed agent retries a bounded number of times, with backoff, and then stops and escalates. The hard case is the request whose outcome is genuinely unknown — the call timed out, or the response was lost in transit. The agent cannot safely assume the first attempt failed. It must reconcile the uncertain outcome before retrying: check the merchant's order state, the commitment record, or the agent's own ledger — but only when that record authoritatively establishes the outcome. A missing response, record, or receipt never means the purchase did not happen, so absence alone is never grounds to retry.

## Why this is different from consumer double-charges

Consumer double-charges are typically a payment-processor bug — the same authorization submitted twice by accident. The consumer notices on their statement and calls the bank. The card network has a straightforward remedy: reverse the duplicate.

Agent double-purchases are structural, not accidental. The agent was designed to retry. The merchant was designed to accept valid requests. The payment rail was designed to settle what it receives. Everyone behaved correctly within their own boundary. The failure lives in the gap between them — the missing record of what the agent was actually trying to commit to.

## The partial fixes that don't fully work

Idempotency keys. The standard remedy for non-idempotent APIs. The client sends a unique key with the request; the server treats duplicate keys as the same request. Durable idempotency keys do work for agents — provided the key is persisted and reused across retries, session restarts, and process boundaries, so the same intent always carries the same key. The failure mode is a regenerated key: if the agent loses the key or creates a fresh one on retry, the server sees a brand-new request. And when the agent cannot tell whether the first request ever arrived, it still needs a reconciliation step, not just a key.

Nonce-based authorization. Payment protocols like EIP-3009 require a unique nonce per authorization. The chain rejects a second settlement with the same nonce. This prevents double-settlement. It does not prevent double-order — the merchant may have already accepted both orders before either authorization reaches the chain.

Spend limits. A cap on total spend per agent per period. This bounds the damage but doesn't prevent the double-purchase itself. It also fails when the double-purchase is within the limit.

Tool-call deduplication. The agent runtime refuses to execute the same tool call twice within a short window. This works when the runtime has a stable view of what "the same tool call" means. It fails when the retry happens across process boundaries, session restarts, or model context resets.

Each of these addresses part of the problem. None addresses the record that makes the duplicate detectable and enforceable in the first place.

## What's actually missing

The missing piece is a commitment identifier that is generated before the purchase attempt and that both the agent and the merchant treat as authoritative.

This is different from an idempotency key. An idempotency key is generated by the client and honored by the server. A commitment identifier is generated as part of the commitment itself — before the agent attempts the purchase, before the merchant receives the request, before either party has committed to anything. It can serve the same deduplication role as an idempotency key when it is durably persisted and reused across retries, while also binding authority, terms, evidence, and recovery.

The commitment record binds:

- The specific intent (what the agent is trying to buy)

- The authority (what the agent is allowed to buy, under what limits)

- The terms (price, deliverable, deadline, acceptance criteria)

- The unique commitment identifier that ties the retry to the original intent

When the agent retries, the retry carries the same commitment identifier. When the merchant receives the second request, it recognizes it as the same commitment. But a commitment ID does not prevent a duplicate by itself — it only makes one detectable. Prevention requires enforcement: the merchant's execution path must perform durable deduplication keyed on that ID before processing, and the payment rail must reject a second settlement of the same authorization. Where the outcome of an attempt is unknown, recovery must reconcile against on-chain state and the commitment record rather than assuming a retry is safe from an absent response.

## How SAAX handles this

SAAX Protocol treats the commitment as the primary artifact of the purchase. The commitment is created before execution begins, and it carries an identifier that survives retries, session restarts, and process boundaries.

A SAAX commitment includes:

- A unique commitment ID, generated at commitment time

- The authority reference (who authorized this commitment and under what scope)

- The terms (what the commitment obligates the parties to)

- The evidence requirements (what counts as fulfillment)

- The recovery policy (what happens if fulfillment fails)

When the same intent is retried, the retry references the same commitment ID. The merchant, the agent, and the settlement rail all work from the same record.

The commitment schema, the lifecycle states, and the evidence interface are documented at saax-protocol.com/spec (/spec). The conformance suite is at saax-protocol.com/conformance (/conformance). For how the same commitment ID is carried in real payments, see the integration guide (/docs).

SAAX runs immediate payments live on Base mainnet, with escrow flows on testnet only — see the current status page (/status) before relying on any flow.

Find SAAX on x402scan: SAAX Router on x402scan (https://www.x402scan.com/server/2836b122-4d1b-4c6f-8ccb-236c539135f8).

# A chain ID is not authorization: verifying Discovery-to-testnet finance

SAAX Protocol · Published November 6, 2026 · Technical implementation note

AI disclosure: this article was researched and written by an AI operator from inspected implementation, executed tests and public-chain evidence. It does not represent an independent audit or a human author's personal test experience.

A provider signs a proposal for Base mainnet. Your test harness switches its RPC to Base Sepolia and checks that the chain ID is 84532. Is that a valid test of the proposal? No. The harness selected a chain; the buyer never authorized that change.

That boundary is easy to miss when connecting signed discovery to payments. Another trap is subtler: a contract can successfully execute a valid evaluator signature while the agreement never authenticated who that evaluator was supposed to be. A receipt proves execution under the contract's stored rules, not that the buyer accepted those rules.

This walkthrough follows SAAX's completed operator-run path from signed Discovery to an authenticated commitment, real Base Sepolia custody funding and a signed release or refund. It also records what the proof does not establish. The public Discovery interfaces are deployed; financial execution remains a testnet preview, not a public escrow service or a mainnet custody launch.

## Keep the authorities separate

The path has several signatures with different meanings:

| Artifact | Authority established | What it does not authorize |
| Provider profile/proposal JWS | A configured provider key signed the supported combinations and offered terms | Buyer consent, token movement or a verdict |
| Buyer acceptance JWS | The registered buyer key accepted the exact proposal and terms digests | Token approval, escrow funding or release |
| Buyer-signed approval/funding transaction | The wallet authorized the specific on-chain action | Proof that work was delivered |
| Seller-signed evidence | The agreed issuer signed a result bound to this request/commitment | Independent service quality or automatic release |
| Evaluator verdict | The agreed evaluator authorized an allowed custody action under its exact domain | Permission from an evaluator not authenticated in the agreement |

A valid JWS signature is also not automatic publisher authentication. The verifier needs an independently configured mapping between provider identity, origin, keyId and public key. The buyer key needs its own registered identity/scope mapping. A public key downloaded beside an untrusted signature proves consistency, not identity. RFC7517's key provenance and trust discussion (https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc7517#section-9.1) is the relevant distinction.

SAAX currently uses configured-key onboarding. It does not claim permissionless publisher authentication. The Discovery quickstart (/docs#discovery-quickstart) explains the boundary and the public nonfinancial operations.

## Bind the selected network and asset before consent

Base's official network details (https://docs.base.org/get-started/connect-to-base) distinguish mainnet 8453 from Base Sepolia 84532. Those identifiers belong inside the authenticated terms, not just an RPC configuration.

The testnet agreement pins this combination:

```
{
"network": "eip155:84532",
"asset": "eip155:84532/erc20:0x036cbd53842c5426634e7929541ec2318f3dcf7e",
"amount": "1000",
"currency": "USDC",
"decimals": 6,
"unit": "micro-units of settlement asset",
"rail": "x402",
"mode": "escrow"
}

```

The amount is 1000 atomic units, or 0.001 test USDC. It never passes through a floating-point currency conversion. rail:x402 is a compatibility label in this profile; mode:escrow explicitly selects custody. The proof does not claim that an x402 facilitator settled this escrow. Immediate x402/x402 requirements are a different signed combination.

A separately signed testnet provider profile declares supported combinations. The provider proposal carries the exact terms and a financialAgreement appointing buyer, seller, evaluator, permitted decisions, custody, token and recovery rules. The buyer acceptance signs the exact termsDigest and proposalDigest. The commitment's provider JWS binds the proposal digest and recomputed manifest, including the relevant versions and evaluator authority.

At handoff, the implementation verifies those records and derives the funding arguments. It does not take a replacement token, network, seller or evaluator from an environment variable. A mainnet-bound proposal attempting testnet execution fails even with a valid signature. A testnet flow pointed at a mainnet RPC also fails. Changing the chain guard cannot change consent; new terms require a new proposal and acceptance.

The old financial exports already named Sepolia in their signed proposal terms. Their deficiency was different: they did not export a separately signed profile or authenticate the concrete financial evaluator and fulfillment chain completely. Those records remain historical evidence with an explicit limitation. Missing authorization cannot be repaired by adding unsigned declarations afterward.

## A local chain named 84532 is still local

A development EVM can be configured with almost any chain ID. Seeing84532 in a local test proves the guard and signature domain used that number. It does not prove the transaction exists on public Base Sepolia.

The fresh proof reads public-chain code, transactions, receipts, execution blocks and historical state through the Base Sepolia RPC. It pins custodyV1 at 0x5a5472d751839cd4968cbf1b136baf862279ff5d and the test-USDC contract. An independent process can inspect the same facts without accessing the application's database.

That still relies on the selected RPC provider. It is not a light-client consensus proof, and it is not a claim that every transaction has reached L1 finality. Finality policy must be stated separately from successful inclusion.

## Reproduce code identity without guessing a metadata trim

A deployment address and a source filename are not enough. Compare the actual runtime to the committed artifact's deployed runtime and a compilation of the exact source bytes with pinned settings.

The custody identity check used solc 0.8.26, optimizer 200, viaIR and Cancun. It reproduced the exact artifact creation code and deployed runtime. Solidity's documented trailer uses the final two bytes as the CBOR metadata length; the checker parses that CBOR map and validates exact consumption. Solidity's metadata documentation (https://docs.soliditylang.org/en/latest/metadata.html#encoding-of-the-metadata-hash-in-the-bytecode) explicitly warns against assuming a fixed layout.

The result is:

```
29 init bytes + 6934 runtime bytes = 6963 creation bytes
6881 executable + 51 CBOR metadata + 2 length bytes = 6934 runtime
runtime keccak256:
0x0897dba060e2c2bd195cc14dc3f3024be465f17107482eb346bde57f56119473

```

An earlier report's 1146-byte metadata trim and 5817-byte executable figure were wrong. Compiling the Windows CRLF checkout changes the metadata hash; compiling the canonical LF Git source reproduces the deployed bytes in full. Constructor arguments are empty, there are no immutable patches or linked libraries, and the contract records its deployment chain ID in storage.

This closes identity, not security. Reproducing unaudited code exactly does not make it audited.

## Treat a transaction hash as a lookup key

Base's receipt reference (https://docs.base.org/base-chain/api-reference/ethereum-json-rpc-api/eth_getTransactionReceipt) returns null for pending/unmined transactions and distinguishes successful status from a revert. A hash by itself proves neither inclusion nor success.

The verifier checks more than status=1:

- The signed transaction chain, destination and referenced receipt/block identity match.

- Funding calldata decodes to the exact commitment digest, token, buyer, seller, evaluator, amount and timing the buyer accepted.

- The custody contract emits the matching Funded event; the pinned token emits the exact buyer-to-custody transfer.

- Terminal calldata calls the expected release/refund function for that same commitment and digest.

- Custody events identify the correct beneficiary, amount and verdict-signature hash; the token transfer and block-pinned balances show the same outcome.

- Historical escrow state moves from Funded to the expected terminal state, at the observed execution time.

ERC-20 defines the Transfer event (https://eips.ethereum.org/EIPS/eip-20#events), but an event signature alone does not identify the token. Validate log.address, indexed parties and amount. The verifier uses actual historical balance reads as corroboration; it does not trust exported “before” balances or require the entire custody contract's current balance to be zero.

For these isolated records, block-level balance deltas agree exactly. A busy shared block could include unrelated transfers; then a verifier needs a suitable transaction-level proof or must report the unsupported case instead of inventing a match.

## Verify the verdict against the deployed contract

EIP-712 (https://eips.ethereum.org/EIPS/eip-712) supplies typed hashing and domain separation. It explicitly does not include replay protection. The contract and verifier need their own action, nonce and timing rules.

CustodyV1 uses:

```
Domain: SAAX Escrow Custody V1 / version 1
chainId: 84532
verifyingContract: 0x5a5472d751839cd4968cbf1b136baf862279ff5d

EscrowVerdict(
bytes32 commitmentId,
bytes32 commitmentDigest,
string action,
uint256 nonce,
uint256 issuedAt
)

```

The independent verifier reads the deployed domain separator, constructor chain and type hash. It decodes the actual transaction's signature fields, recovers the signer and compares it to the evaluator authenticated by the buyer-authorized agreement. It also checks that the agreement permits the action.

Timing is evaluated at the execution block, not at today's wall clock:

```
issuedAt
- Public signed profile, free preflight and configured-buyer commitment creation are deployed beta interfaces; they trigger no financial execution.

- Existing immediate payments are public beta on Base mainnet and remain non-custodial.

- The connected custody flow is an operator-run Base Sepolia testnet preview, not a public financial API or mainnet escrow.

- Specific recovery scenarios have implementation evidence; universal crash recovery and guaranteed refunds are not established.

- Unreleased custody/governance candidates remain under development/security review. External adoption and completed independent audit are not claimed.

## A practical next step

Integrate the public nonfinancial Discovery path (/docs#discovery-quickstart) first: authenticate the provider key independently, request a proposal, verify the exact signed terms, and use an onboarded buyer key for acceptance. Before adding any financial executor, make one negative test pass: a correctly signed mainnet proposal must fail when directed at testnet, without broadcasting anything.

For controlled source access, the financial exports can be checked with:

```
node verifier/verify-financial-export.js \
evidence/discovery-phase6/closeout-release-export.json \
--trust=evidence/discovery-phase6/trust.json --json

```

The trust file must come from your authenticated configuration, not from the untrusted export. Read current status (/status), security (/security) and the versioned specification (/spec) before extending the supported profile. The verifier should tell you precisely where proof ends; your documentation should stop at the same place.

# The Audit Trail Problem in Agentic Commerce

October 8, 2026 · Last updated: 2026-10-17

Six months after an agent made a purchase, someone needs to know what happened.

The buyer wants to reconcile the charge. The merchant wants to prove the fulfillment was correct. A regulator wants to understand how the decision was made. An auditor wants to verify that the transaction complied with the policy that was in force at the time.

Every one of them asks the same question: can you reconstruct what actually happened?

In most agentic commerce systems today, the answer is no.

## Why the record doesn't survive

Agent transactions produce a scattered trail. The agent runtime logs the tool calls. The merchant logs the orders. The payment rail logs the settlements. The model provider may log the prompts, if anything, for a limited window. The authorization system logs the delegation. Each of these records is fragmentary, held by a different party, retained for a different period, and structured differently.

Reconstructing a single transaction across all of them requires the cooperation of every party involved, in a time window before any of them have deleted their logs. In practice, that window closes faster than anyone expects. Log retention policies range from days to months. The agent's session context is gone the moment the process restarts. The model provider's prompts are typically retained for 30 days at most.

Six months later, there is nothing to reconstruct from.

This isn't a storage problem. Storage is cheap. The problem is that no one treated the transaction as a record worth preserving in the first place. Each system recorded what it needed for its own operation, and none of them recorded what would be needed to answer the question that comes later.

## What an audit trail actually requires

An audit trail is not a log. It is a structured, verifiable record that answers the questions a later reviewer will ask. For agentic commerce, those questions are:

- What was authorized? The principal's instruction. The scope granted to the agent. The limits in force at the time.

- What was committed? The specific terms the agent agreed to. Price. Deliverable. Deadline. Acceptance criteria.

- What was executed? The agent's actions. The merchant's fulfillment. The settlement that occurred.

- What proves fulfillment? External evidence that the deliverable matched the acceptance criteria. Independent attestations if applicable.

- What recovery occurred? If something failed, what the recovery policy said, what action was taken, and when the commitment reached finality.

An audit trail is not a single log line. It is a bound record that captures all five of these as a unit, so they can be reviewed together when the question is asked.

## Why existing solutions don't cover this

Application logs capture what an application did. They do not capture the authority under which it acted, the terms it was bound to, or the evidence that supports its claims.

Payment records capture that money moved. They do not capture what the payment was for, whether the deliverable matched the commitment, or what recovery policy applied if it didn't.

Blockchain settlement is immutable but minimal. A transaction hash proves the settlement occurred. It does not prove what the settlement was for.

AP2 and similar protocols define authorization mandates. They record that an agent was authorized to act. They do not record what the agent actually committed to, what was delivered, or how the outcome was verified.

Platform audit logs are held by the platform. They are useful for the platform's own operations. They are not a durable record the buyer, merchant, or regulator can independently verify.

Each captures a piece. None captures the commitment record that makes the transaction reconstructable.

## What SAAX does

SAAX Protocol treats the commitment as the durable unit of record. A commitment captures:

- The authority reference (the proof that the agent was authorized to act)

- The terms (what was promised, at what price, under what constraints)

- The acceptance criteria (what counts as fulfillment)

- The evidence references (what proof was submitted to demonstrate fulfillment)

- The settlement reference (which rail settled, and to what reference)

- The outcome (whether the commitment was fulfilled, failed, or disputed)

- The finality (when the commitment reached its terminal state)

Each commitment is signed and hashed. The record is structured. It survives process restarts, session boundaries, and platform retention policies because it is stored independently of any single party's operational logs.

This does not replace the operational logs of each system. It provides the commitment record that all of them can reference when a later reviewer asks what happened.

## What "durable" actually means

The record has to be durable in three ways:

Structurally durable — the record has a defined schema, not free-form text. A reviewer in six months can read it and understand what happened without needing the original system to explain.

Cryptographically durable — the record is signed by the parties that created it and hashed for integrity. Alteration after the fact is detectable.

Independently durable — the record is not held solely by one party. Any party to the commitment can hold a copy. The absence of one party's storage does not erase the record.

## Why this matters for the parties involved

For the buyer, the record shows what was authorized and what was delivered. If the delivered result does not match the acceptance criteria, the record is the evidence for the recovery claim.

For the merchant, the record shows that fulfillment was performed against a specific commitment with specific terms. The merchant does not carry the liability for a decision that was made against the commitment.

For the platform or rail, the record shows the commitment that the settlement was linked to. The platform does not need to reconstruct what the transaction was for — the commitment record answers it.

For the regulator or auditor, the record is the structured evidence they need to verify that the transaction complied with the policy in force at the time.

## What this looks like in practice

When a SAAX commitment is created, it includes the authority reference, the terms, the acceptance criteria, the evidence requirements, and the recovery policy. This becomes the durable record.

When the commitment is executed, the evidence is attached as references — external attestations, delivery proofs, delivery hashes — signed and bound to the commitment.

When the commitment reaches fulfillment or failure, the outcome and finality states are recorded against the same commitment. The full lifecycle — from authority to finality — is captured in a single durable record.

Six months later, the record still exists only if the parties retained it: the export file, the on-chain anchor, and the evidence material must be available. The on-chain digest and attestation are durable; the full agreement terms and evidence payloads are durable only where the parties keep them (or where the export preserves them). A record that exists only in a worker's memory is not durable. Exporting the commitment and retaining the evidence are part of making the audit trail real.

The spec is at saax-protocol.com/spec (/spec). The conformance suite is at saax-protocol.com/conformance (/conformance). The commitment schema, the evidence interface, and the audit-chain structure are documented there.

# Unknown Payment Outcomes: The Agent Recovery Problem Nobody Instruments

November 4, 2026 · Last updated: 2026-11-04

The most dangerous moment in an agent payment is not the payment. It is the timeout after it.

An agent calls a purchase endpoint. The call times out. The response never arrives. Was the purchase made? The agent does not know. Every reliable-agent tutorial says retry; every commerce system treats the second request as a second purchase. Out of that collision come the duplicate charges, the reconciliation messes, and the "the agent bought it twice" incidents that the retry guidance was supposed to prevent.

## Why unknown outcomes are structural

Unknown outcomes are not a bug in one component. They are the intersection of three reasonable design decisions:

- Agents retry. Network calls fail, timeouts happen, and the standard remedy is a bounded retry with backoff.

- Purchases are not idempotent by default. A second POST to an order API creates a second order unless the server explicitly deduplicates.

- Settlement is asynchronous. The agent's tool call often returns when the order is acknowledged, not when the payment confirms.

The dangerous case is the request whose outcome is genuinely unknown: the call timed out, the response was lost, or the process crashed mid-flight. From the agent's seat, "no response" is indistinguishable from "response lost". Retrying on an absent response is exactly how a double-purchase gets created; assuming the first attempt failed is exactly how a missing record gets declared a non-purchase.

## The partial fixes, and where each stops

- Idempotency keys work for agents provided the key is persisted and reused across retries, session restarts, and process boundaries. The failure mode is a regenerated key: if the agent loses the key or mints a fresh one on retry, the server sees a new request. And when the agent cannot tell whether the first request arrived at all, it still needs reconciliation, not just a key.

- Nonce-based authorization (EIP-3009 style) prevents double-settlement — the chain rejects a second settlement with the same nonce. It does not prevent double-order: the merchant may have accepted both orders before either authorization reaches the chain.

- Spend limits bound the damage. They do not prevent the duplicate, and they fail silently when the duplicate is inside the limit.

- Tool-call deduplication in the agent runtime works when the runtime has a stable view of what "the same tool call" means. It fails across session restarts, process boundaries, and context resets — precisely the boundaries where crashes happen.

Each of these addresses a slice. None addresses the core need: a durable record, created before the attempt, that makes the duplicate detectable and the outcome reconcilable. The double-purchasing failure mode is detailed in Preventing Autonomous Agent Double-Purchasing (/blog/preventing-autonomous-agent-double-purchasing).

## The durable-record pattern

The pattern that survives unknown outcomes has three parts:

- A commitment identifier minted before the attempt. The agent creates a commitment record — intent, authority, terms, acceptance criteria, recovery policy — and receives an ID. Every retry of the same intent carries the same ID.

- Durable deduplication at the execution layer. The merchant's execution path rejects a second request carrying a commitment ID it already processed. An identifier alone does not stop a duplicate; enforcement does.

- Reconciliation of unknown outcomes. When the outcome is unknown, recovery checks on-chain settlement state and the commitment record before deciding whether a retry is safe. Absence of a response is never treated as proof the purchase did not happen.

Step three is the one most systems skip. A missing response, record, or receipt never means the purchase did not happen — so absence alone is never grounds to retry. The correct move is to query the settlement state (did the chain move funds for this reference?) and the commitment state (is there an in-flight commitment with this ID?) before the next attempt.

## How SAAX structures this

SAAX treats the commitment as the primary artifact of the purchase. The commitment is created before execution begins and carries an ID that survives retries, session restarts, and process boundaries; recovery semantics for failure, timeout, partial completion, and dispute are part of the commitment lifecycle (/spec), and the current status page (/status) is explicit that recovery is operator-assisted and demonstrated at specific crash boundaries — not automatic.

That last qualifier matters. A commitment record makes the unknown outcome detectable and gives recovery something durable to reconcile against. It does not by itself guarantee that a hung workflow resumes itself. Anyone evaluating SAAX for agent recovery should read the current status page (/status): immediate x402 payments are public beta on Base mainnet and non-custodial; escrow custody is testnet preview only; a Custody V3 candidate with governance work is under development and has not been independently reviewed.

## Tradeoffs

- Dedup enforcement is a coordination problem. The merchant, the agent, and the settlement rail must all honor the same ID. A commitment ID without enforcement is just a label.

- Reconciliation is only as good as its sources. Checking on-chain state assumes you can read the chain; checking the commitment record assumes the record store survived the crash.

- Bounded retries still need a verdict. At some point the agent must stop and escalate to a human or a recovery process; durable records make that escalation legible, not automatic.

## Where this fits

For a builder wiring agent payments today: persist an idempotency key or commitment ID across process boundaries, make your merchant execution path reject duplicate IDs, and — above all — replace "retry on timeout" with "reconcile, then decide". Treat every unknown outcome as potentially settled until on-chain and commitment state say otherwise.

The commitment schema, lifecycle states, and recovery semantics (/spec) are documented in the SAAX specification, with published conformance vectors (/conformance).

Next step: instrument one of your existing purchase tool calls — before the call, write a commitment/attempt record with a stable ID; on timeout, check the settlement chain and the record before retrying; log what the reconciliation step concluded. Run it against a test endpoint until you see the duplicate case disappear.

# What an AI Agent Payment Authorization Actually Authorizes

SAAX Protocol · Published November 6, 2026 · Technical implementation note

November 6, 2026

A payment authorization is a permission to move money. It is not a contract, a receipt, or proof that work was delivered. The difference decides whether an agent-payment integration can survive a dispute, a retry, or an audit.

The agent-payments products reviewed for this article sell limits: total caps, per-transaction caps, merchant scoping, expiry windows, and approval gates. Those controls answer "how much can this agent spend?" They do not answer the question that matters after the money moves: what did the agent actually commit to, and who is liable when the outcome is wrong? A spend limit bounds the blast radius; it does not define the deal.

## What an authorization is (and is not)

When a human pays a contractor, three things happen that are easy to conflate:

- Authorization — the payer approves a specific payment to a specific payee for a specific purpose.

- Execution — money moves.

- Acceptance of the deal — the payer agrees to the terms of what the payee will deliver.

A payment authorization covers #1 and #2. It is not #3. When an agent pays an API for a "research report", the payment proves the agent's wallet authorized a transfer to that API's address. It does not prove the report was delivered, that the report matched the request, or that the buyer accepted those terms.

This is the failure mode behind most agent-commerce disputes: the payment succeeded, so the seller treats it as acceptance of the work, and the buyer treats it as a down payment on a deliverable. Neither party has a record of what was agreed. The x402 receipt article (/blog/x402-receipts-what-a-receipt-proves) shows why a receipt cannot fill this gap: it proves settlement between two addresses, nothing about the deliverable.

## What the vendor ecosystem actually sells

The current agent-card and spend-management products are honest about their scope. ScopedPay (https://scopedpay.com/) describes "scoped spending authority" with limits, approved merchants, expiry, and an audit trail. PayScope (https://chenruiqi-hash.github.io/payscope/) enforces per-agent spend limits in a smart contract. Agent company-card products (Clink, agentcard.com, and the 2026 wave of finance-team tools) offer per-transaction approvals and JIT funding. IDEMIA's Agentic Commerce announcement likewise centers authentication, spending conditions, and consent at the payment layer.

These are all limit-and-approval systems. They answer "who may spend how much, where, until when." Among the products reviewed for this article, none records what the purchase was for in a way that survives the transaction. A spend limit does not tell you whether the service was delivered; a merchant allowlist does not tell you what the agreed acceptance criteria were; an audit trail of payment events does not tell you what the other side promised.

That is not a criticism of the products. It is a statement of the layer they operate on. The gap is real, and it is the gap a signed commitment record fills.

## The signed-record pattern

The durable alternative is to bind the payment to a record that exists before the money moves and that the payer signs:

- A proposal — the provider states exactly what will be delivered, at what price, in what units, on what network, under what acceptance criteria and recovery rules.

- An acceptance — the buyer signs the exact proposal and terms digest. The signature binds the buyer to that specific content, not to a merchant-scoped allowance or a human-approved limit.

- A commitment — the signed proposal + acceptance produce one verifiable record with a stable ID, carried in the payment's external-reference field and resolved back from the transaction.

The crucial property is domain separation: the authorization to pay, the acceptance of terms, and the later verification of fulfillment are separate signed artifacts with separate meanings. A buyer's acceptance of terms is not a token approval; a payment is not a fulfillment verdict; an evaluator's release verdict is not a payment authorization. Each has its own signature, its own nonce domain, and its own replay rules.

That separation is what makes disputes resolvable. When the buyer and seller disagree, there is a single record both signed that says what was agreed, what counts as done, and what happens on failure. SAAX's implementation (/spec) follows exactly this pattern: prepare_commitment produces a provider-signed proposal; accept_commitment records a buyer-signed acceptance; the commitment binds the two. The walkthrough of the Discovery-to-testnet-finance path (/blog/signed-discovery-to-testnet-finance) shows the same separation in a real flow.

## What an authorization does not solve

Even a perfect signed-commitment record does not remove the need for limits. An agent with a signed commitment can still be compromised, and a spend cap is still the backstop. The mistake is to treat the two as substitutes:

- Limits are a control on the payer. They bound what the agent can do with the wallet.

- Commitments are a control on the deal. They define what the payment was for, so a dispute has a record to resolve against.

You need both. A limit without a commitment leaves you unable to prove what was agreed. A commitment without a limit leaves your wallet exposed to a compromised agent. The architecture guides that separate "commerce discovery from payment execution" and give agents "narrowly scoped identity and budgets" are pointing at the same conclusion from the other side (https://www.casetrue.com/en/articles/ai-agents-spend-money-agentic-commerce-payments-2026): authorization and agreement are different layers.

## Practical guidance

For a developer wiring agent payments today:

- Decide which artifact is authoritative for disputes. If it is the payment receipt, disputes are unresolvable by construction. If it is a signed commitment, make the payment carry the commitment ID (x402's external-reference field, or your own order field) and make your fulfillment path record the commitment ID.

- Separate the signatures. Buyer acceptance of terms should be a distinct signed message from the wallet's payment approval. If you collapse them into one, you cannot distinguish "the buyer agreed to this deal" from "the buyer's wallet paid for something."

- Bind the terms before you bind the money. The acceptance must reference the exact proposal and terms digest. If the terms can change between acceptance and execution, the acceptance means nothing.

- Keep a spend limit as the backstop. The signed record makes the deal legible; the limit makes the wallet survivable. Neither replaces the other.

## Where this fits

The SAAX specification (/spec) defines the commitment lifecycle — authorization, agreement, execution, evidence, outcome verification, settlement, finality, audit — and the Discovery quickstart (/docs#discovery-quickstart) shows the public nonfinancial path: signed profile, free preflight, buyer acceptance, one authenticated commitment. The current status page (/status) is explicit about what is deployed, what is testnet preview, and what remains under review.

The one-line version: an agent payment authorization authorizes a transfer. If you need it to also prove what the deal was, add a signed commitment — because no payment primitive will give you that for free.

AI disclosure: this article was researched and written by an AI operator from publicly available documentation and SAAX's inspected implementation. It does not represent an independent audit or a human author's personal test experience. Verify any protocol claim against the primary specification before relying on it.

Next step: in your next agent-payment integration, add one field to the payment request — a commitment or order ID that the seller's fulfillment path records and the receipt resolves back to. Then, on the next dispute, check whether that ID lets you reconstruct what was agreed. If it does not, you have found the exact gap this article describes.

AI disclosure: this article was researched and written by an AI operator from publicly available documentation and SAAX's inspected implementation. It does not represent an independent audit or a human author's personal test experience. Verify any protocol claim against the primary specification before relying on it.

# What Does an Agent Actually Commit To?

October 10, 2026 · Last updated: 2026-10-17

A payment authorization is a promise to pay. A fulfillment is proof that something was delivered.

Between those two events, something has to define what the agent actually agreed to. Price. Deliverable. Deadline. Acceptance criteria. Evidence requirements. What happens if the delivery fails.

This is the commitment layer, and it's the piece most agent commerce systems are missing.

## Why authorization isn't enough

When a human buys something, the gap between "I authorized this" and "this was delivered correctly" is closed by the human. They know what they wanted. When the goods arrive, they compare. If it doesn't match, they dispute it — and the card network handles it based on the human's testimony.

When an agent is the buyer, none of that works. The agent's intent is not the principal's intent. The record of what the agent was asked to do lives in a prompt log that may expire. The record of what the agent actually did lives in a tool-call log that may not be preserved. The record of what the merchant delivered lives in the merchant's database. None of them reference each other.

Six months later, when someone asks what happened, the answer is: you can't reconstruct it.

## What a commitment records

A commitment binds five things before execution begins:

Authority — who authorized the agent to act, under what scope, with what limits. This is the proof that the agent was permitted to enter the commitment.

Terms — what was agreed. Price, deliverable, deadline, and the specific conditions under which the commitment is fulfilled.

Acceptance criteria — what objectively counts as fulfillment. Not "the merchant says it shipped" but "the evidence shows the item matched the specified criteria."

Evidence requirements — what proof must be submitted to demonstrate fulfillment. External attestations, delivery hashes, signed receipts, or sensor data depending on the domain.

Recovery policy — what happens if fulfillment fails. Refund, compensation, dispute, or escalation. Set at commitment time, not negotiated after the problem emerges.

## The lifecycle

A commitment has states. It moves through them, and each state has defined transitions:

COMMITTED → EXECUTING → FULFILLED

or

COMMITTED → EXECUTING → FAILED → RECOVERY → DISPUTE → RESOLVED → FINAL

Failure doesn't terminate the commitment. It moves it into a recovery state where the recovery policy applies. External systems handle the refund, the compensation, or the arbitration. The commitment records what was required, what failed, what action occurred, and when the commitment became final.

## The in-flight problem

The hardest state is in_flight — the window where the merchant has received the commitment but the agent hasn't yet received confirmation.

If the agent's first attempt times out, it can't know whether the merchant never received it or is processing it right now. A naive retry with the same commitment ID races the merchant's accept path and creates a duplicate.

The protocol rule is simple: an unknown outcome is a status check, not another POST. This rule is safe only when the status check can determine the real outcome — from durable state or from the chain. Where the broadcast reference was never durably recorded (the broadcast-before-durable-hash gap), an absent record is not proof that a retry is safe; the outcome must be determined from the chain before retrying.

The agent queries the commitment state before retrying. not_found means safe to retry. in_flight means wait. fulfilled means stop. failed means retry with a fresh commitment ID.

On the merchant side, the rule is equally clear: the merchant writes in_flight to durable storage before processing the request. The write is the lock. A second request with the same commitment ID returns in_flight — it isn't processed again.

Both sides need both rules. Neither alone closes the gap.

## Why this matters for the parties involved

For the buyer — the commitment is the evidence. If the delivered result doesn't match the acceptance criteria, the commitment is what proves it.

For the merchant — the commitment shows that fulfillment was performed against specific terms. The merchant doesn't carry the liability for a decision that was made against the commitment.

For the platform or rail — the commitment links the settlement to the agreement it was for. The platform doesn't need to reconstruct what the transaction was about.

For the regulator or auditor — the commitment is the structured record that makes the transaction verifiable and reconstructable.

## What this isn't

A commitment layer is not a payment rail, an identity provider, or an oracle. It doesn't replace x402, MPP, AP2, or the card networks. It sits above them.

The payment layer proves the transaction was permitted. The commitment layer proves the transaction delivered what it was supposed to.

Authorization is not fulfillment. The two are treated as equivalent in most commerce infrastructure, and that assumption breaks the moment an agent is on the other end of the purchase.

The spec is at saax-protocol.com/spec (/spec). The conformance suite is at saax-protocol.com/conformance (/conformance). The commitment schema, the lifecycle states, and the in-flight handling rule are documented there.

# What a Smart Contract Escrow Security Review Actually Verifies

SAAX Protocol · Published November 6, 2026 · Technical implementation note

November 6, 2026

A smart contract escrow review is not a checklist of vulnerability classes. It is a verification that the contract's authorization model matches the deal the parties agreed to — and that no configuration can permanently lock the funds.

Escrow reviews can fail not because reentrancy was missed, but because the reviewer checked the wrong question. The generic vulnerability lists answer "can an attacker drain the contract?" The escrow-specific question is narrower and harder: "can the contract release the funds to the right party, at the right time, under the right authorization — and only then?" This article walks through what an escrow review must actually verify, using SAAX's real review-scope documents as a worked example.

## Why "audit checklist" is the wrong mental model

The 2026 OWASP Smart Contract Top 10 ranks Access Control Vulnerabilities at #1 (https://scs.owasp.org/sctop10/SC01-AccessControlVulnerabilities/), ahead of business logic and reentrancy. But "access control" in an escrow is not a boolean — it is a chain of authorization: who may fund, who may release, who may refund, who may dispute, who may evaluate, and under what conditions each action is legal. An audit checklist that flags "missing access control" is useless unless it also verifies the escrow's specific rules: the timed release, the cutoff semantics, the evaluator's powers, the dispute path, and the liveness of every legitimate exit.

The OWASP SCSVS (https://scs.owasp.org/) and the Smart Contract Top 10 (https://scs.owasp.org/sctop10/) correctly point at the classes — access control, business logic, reentrancy, oracle manipulation, input validation. What they do not provide is a per-domain checklist for escrow, because escrow is a business-logic-heavy domain where the semantics matter more than the vulnerability class.

## The escrow-specific verification scope

A reviewer of an escrow contract must verify, in order:

1. The authorization chain. Every state transition needs an explicit, authenticated actor:

- Who can fund? (buyer only, with the exact agreement digest?)

- Who can release to the seller? (evaluator-signed verdict only? buyer+seller mutual?)

- Who can refund? (evaluator-signed refund, or buyer after deadline, or timeout?)

- Who can raise a dispute? (buyer or seller only?)

- What happens if the evaluator disappears? (funds frozen forever = a finding)

2. Timed release and cutoff semantics. Escrow is about when, not just who. The review must check:

- The deadline math (is deadline inclusive? is now > deadline or now >= deadline?)

- Whether release is possible before the deadline, after the cutoff, or in the "dead window" between the two

- Whether a timeout refund is only available while Funded (not while Disputed)

- What resolve("hold") means at or after cutoff — is that a permanent lock?

3. Evaluator authority. The crux of escrow:

- Is the evaluator identity authenticated in the agreement (not just in the contract's storage)?

- Are the evaluator's permitted decisions scoped — can it release, refund, both, or resolve-hold?

- Is the verdict signature bound to the exact EIP-712 domain: chain ID, contract address, struct type, action, nonce, issuedAt?

- Is the verdict valid at the execution block's timestamp, not just at signing time?

4. Replay and nonce separation. The review must confirm distinct nonce domains for distinct action classes (verdict vs. mutual vs. access), so a release verdict cannot be replayed as a refund, and a cross-chain replay is prevented by chain-ID binding.

5. Reentrancy and CEI order. In every transition, state must be written before external calls, and the checks-effects-interactions pattern must hold in every path — including refund and resolve.

6. Token handling. Exactly-once payouts assume standard tokens. The review must decide whether fee-on-transfer, rebasing, or pausable tokens are supported or must be whitelisted — and whether a payout's "balance delta vs. transfer amount" check is sound.

7. Dispute liveness. The worst escrow outcome is a permanent lock. The review must verify every configuration has at least one legitimate exit, and flag any path where funds can be frozen indefinitely (e.g., evaluator disappearance while Disputed).

## Concretely: SAAX's review snapshot

SAAX's custody candidate (Custody V3, SAAXEscrowCustodyV3.sol (/status)) is currently the subject of a real review-scope exercise. The owner-approved review snapshot (/status) pins the candidate source, artifact, and test evidence (manifest SHA-256 920ddff8…) as the baseline for independent review. The reviewer handoff (/status) is explicit that the snapshot is approved for review only — not an audit, not production readiness, not deployment approval.

The review scope document lists exactly the checks above: accounting/conservation, terminal exclusivity, CEI order, safe-transfer handling, funding gates, cutoff semantics, verdict/mutual authorization, ERC-1271 evaluator container + EOA path, replay guards (separate verdict/mutual nonces), resolve-hold + cutoff interplay, min-release-time coverage, and dispute paths. It also lists the open questions the reviewer must answer: authorization timing (is execution-point authorization sufficient, or is post-block governance-state verification required?), same-block ordering robustness against reorg, token whitelist necessity, reentrancy confirmation, cross-chain replay protection, and dispute liveness (can any configuration permanently lock funds?).

That is the shape of a serious escrow review: not "we checked for reentrancy" but "here are the authorization-chain, timing, and liveness questions, and here is what must be true for each."

## The critical distinction: review snapshot ≠ audit ≠ readiness

The most common misunderstanding in escrow-review communication is conflating the preparation with the verification. An owner-approved snapshot for independent review means:

- The exact bytes (source, artifact, evidence) are frozen as the baseline.

- A reviewer can rely on those pinned bytes.

- It does not mean the review has happened, that findings are resolved, or that the contract is safe to deploy.

SAAX's status page is explicit: "Custody V3 has an owner-approved snapshot for independent review; that review has not been completed. It is not an audit, not production readiness, and not deployment approval." Anyone publishing a review snapshot should say the same. The moment a project blurs "we prepared a review package" into "we were reviewed," the entire exercise loses its value.

## What the review cannot cover

Every escrow review has explicit exclusions, and a good review-scope document names them:

- The payment rail (x402 lane), the website, and the OS/host are outside the contract review.

- Third-party internals (Safe governance, RPC providers, token behavior) are trust assumptions, not verified facts.

- A code match establishes identity, not safety: "the deployed runtime equals the reviewed artifact" is necessary, but it is not "the contract is safe."

- Local test counts and local anchors are not public-chain finality.

- The verifier's execution-witness model (trusted-RPC consensus-status assertion) is a documented limitation, not a proof of L1 finality.

## Practical guidance

If you are commissioning or writing an escrow review:

- Scope the authorization chain first. Write the "who may do what, when, under what signature" table before any code review. If you cannot write that table, the contract is not reviewable.

- Ask the timing questions. Deadline vs. cutoff, the dead window, resolve-hold semantics, and timeout-refund-while-funding-only are escrow-specific and are where the worst bugs hide.

- Verify the verdict's domain binding. Chain ID, contract address, struct, action, nonce, issuedAt — any one missing enables replay or cross-contract confusion.

- Test dispute liveness explicitly. Add a test case for "evaluator disappears while Disputed." If funds freeze forever, that is a finding even if no vulnerability class matches.

- Separate the snapshot from the verdict. Publish the frozen baseline with its manifest hash, state clearly that review has not concluded, and never call an approved snapshot an audit.

## Where this fits

SAAX's security page (/security) documents the exact deployed testnet CustodyV1 identity (runtime 0x5a5472…, 6934 bytes: 6881 executable + 51 CBOR metadata + 2 length bytes), the pinned-solc reproduction, and the hard line that "a code match establishes identity, not safety." The current status page (/status) distinguishes the deployed testnet contract from the unreleased V3 candidate and keeps the review-snapshot wording precise. The integration guide (/docs) and specification (/spec) define the commitment lifecycle an escrow review must be checked against.

The one-line version: an escrow security review verifies the authorization chain, the timing semantics, the evaluator's domain-bound powers, the replay protection, and the liveness of every legitimate exit — and a review snapshot is the starting line for that verification, never the finish.

AI disclosure: this article was researched and written by an AI operator from publicly available documentation and SAAX's inspected implementation. It does not represent an independent audit or a human author's personal test experience. Verify any protocol claim against the primary specification before relying on it.

Next step: take whichever escrow contract you depend on and write its "who may do what, when, under what signature" table today. If any row is ambiguous — the deadline math, the evaluator's scope, or the dispute path — that ambiguity is your first review finding, whether or not you have hired an auditor yet.

# Agentic Commerce Foundations: The Complete Guide

October 11, 2026 · Last updated: 2026-10-17

Agentic commerce is the practice of an AI agent completing part or all of a purchase on a person's behalf. Instead of you searching for a product, reading reviews, and buying it, you tell an assistant what you want and it does the work.

The demand signal is hard to ignore. US searches for "agentic commerce" are up 408% year on year. But the category is still early — most purchases are still human, and the infrastructure to make agent commerce trustworthy is still being built.

## The two sides of agentic commerce

Consumer-facing agents are the ones most people have heard of. You tell ChatGPT, Gemini, or Claude what you want to buy, and the agent researches, compares, and potentially completes the purchase. Google has been folding agentic checkout into AI Mode and AI Overviews. Shopify, Etsy, Wayfair, Target, and Walmart have all signed on to Google's Universal Commerce Protocol (UCP) to make their products discoverable by agents.

Business-facing agents are where the real volume exists today. Companies are deploying agents for procurement, research, data processing, and vendor management. The agents transact with external services — API calls, data lookups, subscriptions — and the payment rails to support this are maturing fast.

The distinction matters because the trust threshold is different. A consumer letting an agent buy a $50 product is a different risk profile from a business letting an agent commit to a $5,000 contract.

## The protocols trying to define how agents pay

Four major protocols are competing to become the standard for agent payments:

AP2 (Agent Payments Protocol). Google's protocol, launched with 60+ partners including Mastercard, PayPal, American Express, and Coinbase. AP2 introduces Verifiable Credentials — Intent Mandates, Cart Mandates, and Payment Mandates — that cryptographically capture user authorization and intent. The goal is to solve the "crisis of trust" inherent in autonomous agent payments.

x402. Coinbase's protocol, released four months before AP2 appeared. It revives HTTP status code 402 ("Payment Required") and makes payment a native HTTP operation. Request a paid resource, receive a 402 response with payment terms, send payment, get the resource. By October 2025, x402 processed 500,000 weekly transactions.

ACP (Agentic Commerce Protocol). OpenAI and Stripe's protocol, currently in beta. It defines the Agentic Checkout Specification (ACS) as a REST API contract for agents to complete purchases. The merchant remains the system of record — same principle as UCP, but more focused on the checkout flow.

UCP (Universal Commerce Protocol). Google's broader commerce protocol, co-developed with Shopify, Etsy, Wayfair, Target, and Walmart. UCP lets merchants declare their capabilities (product listing, cart management, checkout, returns) through a standardized profile, and agents discover those capabilities dynamically.

## The gap none of them close

Each of these protocols handles a different piece of the agent commerce stack. AP2 handles authorization. x402 handles settlement. ACP handles checkout. UCP handles capability discovery.

None of them handle the commitment layer — the structured record of what the agent actually agreed to, what counts as fulfillment, and what happens when fulfillment fails.

This is the gap that matters when something goes wrong. A signed payment mandate proves the transaction was permitted. It does not prove the deliverable matched the agreement. When an agent buys wrong, there's no structured record to resolve the dispute against.

## What agentic commerce needs to scale

The infrastructure exists. The demand is growing. The missing piece is trust — the ability for a buyer to enter a transaction with an agent they've never used before and know that the outcome is verifiable.

That's what a commitment layer adds. It records the authority, terms, acceptance criteria, evidence requirements, and recovery policy before execution begins. A commitment ID can prevent double-charging only when the settlement layer enforces durable deduplication — the same ID must be recognized as the same intent and the same payment authorization must not settle twice. If the fulfillment doesn't match the agreement, the commitment record is the evidence.

For the integration details, see the integration guide (/docs): MCP connection, immediate x402 payments on Base mainnet, and the testnet-only escrow flow. For a closer look at the individual protocols, see Agentic Commerce Protocols Explained: AP2, x402, ACP, and UCP (/blog/agentic-commerce-protocols-explained), which compares what each one handles and what it does not. The spec is at saax-protocol.com/spec (/spec) and the conformance suite at saax-protocol.com/conformance (/conformance); the commitment lifecycle, the evidence interface, and the settlement-linkage model are documented there.
