Source: https://saax-protocol.com/blog/why-payment-authorization-does-not-equal-fulfillment

# Why Payment Authorization ≠ Fulfillment in Agentic Commerce

October 8, 2026 · Last updated: 2026-10-17

A payment authorization is a promise to pay. A fulfillment is proof that something was delivered.

The two are treated as equivalent in most commerce infrastructure. The authorization clears, the settlement occurs, and the transaction is considered complete. This works when a human is on the other end of the purchase — they authorized the transaction, they received the goods, and their own judgment closes the gap.

When an agent is on the other end, the gap doesn't close. The agent authorized the transaction. The payment cleared. The merchant shipped something. But whether that something matches what the agent actually intended to buy is a separate question — and no layer in the stack is designed to answer it.

## What payment protocols actually prove

A payment authorization proves one thing: at a specific moment, some party with valid credentials authorized a transfer of value to another party.

That is the entire claim. It does not prove:

- That the authorizing party understood what they were authorizing

- That the recipient was capable of delivering what was paid for

- That the deliverable matched any acceptance criteria

- That the transaction was not duplicated

- That the merchant's claim of fulfillment is true

- That any recovery process exists if the fulfillment fails

These are not edge cases. They are the ordinary questions that arise in commerce, and the payment layer answers none of them.

## Why this was fine before agents

For a human-driven purchase, the gap between authorization and fulfillment is closed by the human. The buyer knows what they intended to buy. When the goods arrive, the buyer compares the goods to the intent. If they don't match, the buyer initiates a dispute — which the card network handles based on the human's testimony.

The card network's dispute infrastructure assumes a human is available to testify. It assumes the human's intent is knowable because the human is the one who authorized the transaction. It assumes the record of the intent is the human's word.

When an agent is the authorizer, none of these assumptions hold. The agent's intent is not equivalent to the principal's intent. The record of what the agent was asked to do lives in a prompt log that may expire. The record of what the agent actually did lives in a tool-call log that may not have been preserved. The record of what the merchant delivered lives in the merchant's database. None of these records necessarily reference each other.

When the human buyer calls their bank to dispute the charge, they can say "I never asked for this." When the principal behind an agent calls their bank, they have to say "I asked the agent to do something, and the agent did something different, and here is the record that proves it." For most agent systems, that record does not exist.

## Why stablecoin rails make it worse

Card networks at least have a dispute layer. Stablecoin rails generally don't: settlement is final the moment the transaction confirms, with no built-in reversal mechanism. That does not mean value can never move back — the parties can voluntarily transfer funds, and in SAAX's testnet escrow flow the custody contract can transfer funds back to the buyer under an evaluator-signed refund verdict. But that is a separate, conditional transfer, not a reversal of the blockchain record, and it is not guaranteed. On mainnet immediate payments, settlement is final.

This is not a design flaw in stablecoin rails. It is a design property. The entire point of a stablecoin is that settlement is final. The point of a card authorization is that settlement can be reversed under specific conditions. These are different products serving different use cases.

But agents are increasingly being deployed on stablecoin rails for the same reasons they're deployed everywhere — programmable, fast, low-fee, no banking hours. When agent commerce runs on rails that have no dispute mechanism, the gap between authorization and fulfillment becomes permanent.

## The three-layer model that's missing

Agent commerce requires three distinct layers, and most implementations collapse them into one:

Authorization — proves that a party with valid credentials authorized a specific transfer of value. This is what x402, MPP, and the card networks handle.

Commitment — binds the specific terms of what was agreed. Price, deliverable, deadline, acceptance criteria, evidence requirements, recovery policy. This is the layer that does not exist in most agent commerce systems today.

Settlement — moves the value on the specified rail. This is what the payment processors handle.

Most systems today have authorization and settlement. The commitment layer — the one that records what was agreed and evaluates whether the agreement was fulfilled — is missing.

Without the commitment layer, the payment layer is trying to do the work of the commitment layer. It approves transactions it should not approve, and it disputes transactions it cannot evaluate. It has no basis for either decision because it was never given the terms.

## What SAAX does

SAAX Protocol defines the commitment layer as a distinct artifact from the authorization and the settlement.

A commitment binds:

- The authority reference (who authorized this commitment, under what scope)

- The terms (what was agreed, at what price, by what deadline)

- The acceptance criteria (what counts as fulfillment)

- The evidence requirements (what proof must be submitted)

- The recovery policy (what happens if fulfillment fails)

- The settlement reference (which rail settles this commitment, and to what reference)

The authorization and settlement happen on the rails the parties have chosen. The commitment is the record that binds them together — and the record that determines whether the fulfillment matched the agreement.

This is not a replacement for x402, MPP, or the card networks. It is the layer above them — the layer that answers the question the payment layer cannot: did the fulfillment match the commitment?

The spec is at saax-protocol.com/spec (/spec). The conformance suite is at saax-protocol.com/conformance (/conformance). The commitment schema, the evidence interface, and the settlement-linkage model are documented there.

# x402 Receipts: What a Payment Receipt Actually Proves

November 4, 2026 · Last updated: 2026-11-04

An x402 receipt proves that payment moved. It does not prove that anything was delivered.

That distinction decides how much you can rely on a receipt in an agent workflow. A paid HTTP call returns a response, a payment signature, and an on-chain transaction. Collectively these are the receipt. They prove a settlement occurred between two addresses at a point in time. They do not prove the deliverable matched the terms, that the seller's claim of fulfillment is true, or that the purchase was not duplicated.

## What an x402 payment actually returns

x402 turns the dormant HTTP 402 status code into a payment flow: a client requests a resource, the server responds with a Payment Required challenge describing what to pay and to whom, the client settles, and the server returns the resource. The protocol documentation (https://docs.x402.org/introduction) is explicit that the challenge describes a payment, not a delivery.

x402 V2 moved the payment data into headers (PAYMENT-REQUIRED, PAYMENT-RESPONSE, PAYMENT-SIGNATURE) so the response body stays available for the resource itself, and it adds lifecycle hooks — including before/after settlement verification — so integrators can capture and validate a receipt at the moment payment confirms (x402 V2 announcement (https://x402.org/x402-v2-launch/)). With V1, integrators had to parse the challenge and the settlement response themselves; V2 gives the SDK a place to hook verification logic.

What an integrator typically stores as a "receipt":

- The PAYMENT-RESPONSE / signature data returned by the server or facilitator

- The settlement transaction hash on the settlement chain

- The seller's fulfillment response (the body that came with the 200)

The first two are payment evidence. The third is a claim.

## What a receipt can be checked against

The useful property of an on-chain receipt is that it can be re-verified by a third party without trusting the agent or the seller. Tools in the ecosystem do exactly this: vet402 (https://vet402.com/) re-reads the settlement transfer on-chain and separates "the server said the payment wall passed" from "the transfer actually confirmed", and x402-attest (https://github.com/0xsims/x402-attest) issues tamper-evident receipts for paid HTTP calls that a third party can verify without trusting the involved parties.

This works because the settlement reference — chain, asset, amount, sender, recipient, transaction hash — is public. Anyone can replay the read against a block explorer or an RPC and confirm the value moved.

That is the ceiling of a receipt: it proves a transfer. Everything above it is inference.

## What a receipt does not prove

A settlement reference says nothing about:

- Fulfillment. The seller may have taken the payment and returned garbage. The receipt is silent.

- Authorization of the action. A settled payment is not an authorized action. The authorization question — was the buyer's agent permitted to make this purchase — lives in a different layer (AP2-style mandates, verifiable intent, or a commitment's authority reference), not in the transfer.

- Non-duplication. Two separate settlements to the same seller are two receipts. Nothing in either receipt says the second was a mistake.

- Deliverable quality. A receipt cannot carry acceptance-criteria evaluation; that requires evidence, not payment.

The x402 spec does not claim otherwise. The gap appears when an agent pipeline treats "receipt present" as "transaction complete". That conflation is where wrong purchases, duplicates, and dispute failures come from. The recovery side of that problem is covered in Unknown Payment Outcomes: The Agent Recovery Problem Nobody Instruments (/blog/unknown-payment-outcomes-agent-recovery).

## The receipt-to-commitment pattern

The pattern that closes the gap is to bind the receipt to a commitment record created before the purchase attempt.

A commitment record — the kind SAAX defines — holds the authority reference, terms, acceptance criteria, evidence requirements, recovery policy, and the settlement reference of the payment. When the agent pays, the receipt is attached as the settlement evidence for that commitment. Verification then has a shape: does this settlement reference match the commitment's agreed price, recipient, and terms? Is the evidence genuine? Is the outcome consistent with the acceptance criteria?

SAAX's current implementation reflects this split. Receipt lookup by transaction hash is available at /receipt, and the MCP server exposes evidence and authority verification tools; the supported evidence schemes are eip712, cose, and jws (with cose/jws validated structurally, without an attesting verifier — see the current status page (/status)). A receipt confirms a settlement reference; the status page says so explicitly: it does not prove fulfillment or independently verify the full lifecycle.

One operational caveat that is current as of this writing: the live receipt lookup at /receipt is erroring on a store schema mismatch. The MCP verification and commitment APIs are unaffected. Anyone building on receipt lookup today should read the current status page (/status) before relying on it.

## Tradeoffs

- Facilitator trust. When a facilitator settles on the server's behalf, the receipt's authenticity depends on the facilitator's signing key and the server's honesty. Structural validation is not attestation.

- Chain finality. A receipt is only as final as the settlement chain. On Base mainnet, USDC settlement is irreversible once confirmed; there is no chargeback layer underneath the receipt.

- Receipt vs. evidence. A receipt is settlement evidence. Fulfillment evidence — the artifact that proves delivery matched the terms — is a separate record with its own verification requirements (freshness, issuer, criteria), as defined in the commitment lifecycle specification.

## Where this fits

For a developer wiring agent payments today, the practical rule: capture the signed payment response and the transaction hash at settlement time, verify the transfer independently against the chain, and store the receipt against the commitment that authorized the purchase. Do not let a receipt stand in for fulfillment evidence.

SAAX publishes the commitment schema, the evidence interface, and the settlement-linkage model (/spec) in the specification, and the conformance suite (/conformance) pins down the tested behavior.

Next step: build a small capture-and-verify loop — pay for one test resource over x402 on Base Sepolia, save the PAYMENT-RESPONSE and the transaction hash, and re-verify the transfer from the hash before you attach it to anything you consider a completed transaction.
